family: All four are hypotenuses of integer right triangles: 13 (5-12-13), 15 (9-12-15), 20 (12-16-20), 29 (20-21-29). Asking 'which is the Pythagorean-looking number?' returns four.
tension: Rule 6 fully satisfied, but at the cost of rule 5: the only triple hypotenuses BELOW 13 are 5 and 10, and both are barred by rule 2 (5 is a leg of the figure, 10 is double it). The key is forced to rank 1. Rules 2 and 6 are jointly satisfiable here; rules 2, 5 and 6 are not.

family: All four are leg-over-hypotenuse ratios of primitive Pythagorean triples, so each is a legitimate cosine of an integer-sided right triangle: 4/5 (3-4-5), 5/13 (5-12-13), 15/17 (8-15-17), 24/25 (7-24-25). All lie strictly in (0,1), so rule 3 holds — this fixes the round-1 defect where two options exceeded 1. No two options are the sine/cosine of the same angle (no complementary pair), which would itself have been a structural tell.

Small negative integers, i.e. clean y-intercepts of a parabola drawn on an integer grid. There is no 'famous value' axis for a y-intercept, so equal canonicality means equal integrality and equal magnitude — no option is a rounder number than another. Deliberately all the same sign: a lone positive among negatives would be eliminable from the parabola's visible position alone.

All four are hypotenuses of integer right triangles, three of them 3-4-5 scalings: 50 (30-40-50), 45 (27-36-45), 55 (33-44-55), 65 (39-52-65, also 16-63-65). This is the property that made the original #4 the one item neither attack cracked, applied deliberately rather than by accident.

All four are integer lattice-point distances that arise from a Pythagorean triple: 5 (3-4), 10 (6-8), 13 (5-12), 15 (9-12). Chosen over larger triple hypotenuses so the magnitudes stay close enough that a sighted student cannot eliminate by eyeballing the plot.
tension: Rule 5 sacrificed, not rule 2 or 6. Below 5 the only same-family values are 3 and 4 — the legs themselves, i.e. exactly the round-1 disclosure. The key cannot be moved off rank 1 without either leaking an operand or breaking the family.

family: All four are triple hypotenuses / integer lattice distances: 10 (6-8), 13 (5-12), 15 (9-12), 17 (8-15). None of 13, 15, 17 is reachable from 6 and 8 by sum (14), difference (2), product (48), square (36/64), half, double, or mean (7) — the four operations that leaked this item in round 1.
tension: Rule 5 sacrificed. The only same-family value below 10 is 5, which is simultaneously half the key and sqrt-adjacent to the legs; using it would reinstate the round-1 leak. Rank 1 is forced.

family: Small negative integers of comparable size — every one of them is an equally clean y-value for a line read off an integer grid at x = 6. No option is a multiple, half or negation of another, so none stands out as 'the constructed one'. Deliberately a different set from the other -6 item so the two do not share an option signature.

Plain small integers. Power-of-a-point items have no famous-value family — any integer AB is equally canonical — so equal recognisability is achieved by making no option arithmetically special. Every option excluded that touches the hidden lengths PT = 6, PA = 4, PB = 9: 3 (PB-PT), 9 (PB), 13 (PA+PB), 10 (PA+PT), 15 (PT+PB), 2 (PT-PA), 8 (2*PA), 12 (2*PT), 6 (PT).
tension: Rule 5 sacrificed. Reaching rank 3 or 4 needs two or three options below 5, and of {1,2,3,4} every value except 1 is a difference or a copy of a hidden length; 1 alone would read as degenerate and be eliminable on sight. Rank 1 is the only rule-2-clean choice.

family: All four are integers that are the geometric mean of an integer pair, i.e. legitimate altitudes to a hypotenuse split into integer segments: 6 = sqrt(3*12), 2 = sqrt(1*4), 5 = sqrt(1*25), 8 = sqrt(4*16). Critically, no option is the ARITHMETIC mean of the same hidden pair (7.5) or their sum (15) — the round-1 leak — and none is 9 = 12-3, which round 2 left in.
tension: Minor rule-2 note, not a sacrifice: 4 would have been the natural fourth same-family value but 4 = 12/3, a single quotient of the two hidden segments, so it was dropped in favour of 2.

family: All four are triple hypotenuses / integer lattice distances: 13 (5-12), 10 (6-8), 15 (9-12), 20 (12-16).
tension: Rule 2 partially sacrificed, deliberately, to buy rule 5. 10 = 2 * 5 is double one of the hidden legs. It was admitted because the alternative was a CROSS-ITEM tell: this item and item 0088dae3 share the key 13 and the same family, and if both put the key at rank 1 a solver learns 'the smallest triple hypotenuse is the answer' across the batch. The disclosure risk is low because 10 is a self-standing triple hypotenuse (6-8-10), not a recognisable mis-computation of 5-12-13 — round 1's leak worked because each distractor announced itself as a named error, and 'double one leg' is not an error a solver expects the author to have modelled.

family: Plain small positive integers, all equally clean readings of a line at x = 6 on an integer grid. Excluded 3 and 18 (half and double the key), 6 (the x-value in the stem, which would look like a slope-1 trap) and 12 (2*6).

All four are legs of integer right triangles, which is exactly what a centre-to-chord distance is (leg of the right triangle radius / half-chord / distance): 12 (9-12-15), 5 (5-12-13), 8 (8-15-17), 10 (10-24-26). Excluded 9 and 15 (the half-chord and the radius themselves — round 2 left both in), 6 and 24 (half and double the key).
